findings.claim: They divide into two groups: the first four concern the relationship between humanity and God (no other gods; no idols; not taking God's name in vain; keeping Shabbat holy), and the remaining six concern the relationship between people (honour your parents; do not murder; ...).
findings.truth: That is the Christian (Protestant) enumeration, taught here as Jewish. Jewish tradition divides the Ten Sayings five and five: the first five are duties owed to God and include 'I am the Lord your God' as the opening saying and 'Honour your father and mother'; the second five are duties owed to other people. The Talmud likens honouring parents to honouring God, which is why it sits on the first tablet. The error also contradicts the collapsible later in the same lesson, which teaches bein adam l'Makom and bein adam l'chavero.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Ten Commandments' (Talmudic column; Rabbi Hanina ben Gamaliel: each tablet held five commandments); Wikipedia 'Honour thy father and thy mother' (the Talmud compares the honour owed to parents with the honour owed to God); spec 3.1.6.1 'Mitzvot between man and God and mitzvot between man and man'

findings.claim: 'Give two attributes of God in Jewish teaching.' labelled '2 marks - State / Give', mark scheme '1 mark for each correct attribute, up to 2 marks'.
findings.truth: This paper sets no 2-mark question. Each religion is examined by two five-part questions of 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12 marks, so the short-answer part is worth 1 mark for one item.

findings.claim: 'Give two reasons why this belief might bring comfort to Daniel's family.' labelled '2 marks - State / Give'.
findings.truth: Same as F2: no 2-mark question exists on this paper. One item, 1 mark.

findings.claim: 'Give two promises God made to Abraham in Genesis 12:1-3.' labelled '2 marks - State / Give'.
findings.truth: Same as F2: no 2-mark question exists on this paper. One item, 1 mark.

findings.claim: 'Give two ways in which the principle of Pikuach Nefesh affects Jewish life in practice.' labelled '2 marks - State / Give'.
findings.truth: Same as F2: no 2-mark question exists on this paper. One item, 1 mark.

findings.claim: Four core moral principles run through Jewish ethical teaching and appear explicitly in the Torah and the prophetic tradition: tzedek (justice), tikkun olam (healing the world), tzedakah (charity) and chesed (loving kindness).
findings.truth: Tikkun olam does not appear in the Torah or in the prophets. The phrase comes from the Aleinu prayer and from rabbinic law (mipnei tikkun ha-olam); its social-justice meaning is modern, and the lesson itself says so two paragraphs later ('particularly in Reform and Liberal communities' in the modern period). A student who writes 'the Torah says tikkun olam' cannot support it. Dropping the source claim leaves the four principles, which match the spec wording exactly.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.6.1 'Key moral principles including justice, healing the world, charity and kindness to others'; internal contradiction with the tikkun olam section of the same lesson

findings.claim: The same teaching is cited two different ways inside one lesson: 'Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 4:9' in the content, the key fact and a flashcard, but 'Sanhedrin 37a' in the conclusion, the exam tip, two practice mark schemes and a knowledge check.
findings.truth: Both references are real (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, parallel at Bavli Sanhedrin 37a and Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 4:9), so neither is false, but a student revising this lesson cannot tell which to quote and the knowledge check tests only one of them. Standardise on Talmud, Sanhedrin 37a, which is the citation the rest of the lesson already uses.
findings.evidence: internal inconsistency; standard citation pair Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 / Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 37a

findings.claim: 'Give two contrasting Jewish beliefs about the Messiah.' is labelled '4 marks - Explain' and its mark scheme awards '1 mark for each belief identified, 1 mark for each belief developed'.
findings.truth: The command word does not match the marks. A student who follows 'Give' will name two beliefs and lose the two development marks. The 4-mark part asks students to explain.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section, lines 1826-1836 (AO1 across the first four parts); internal mismatch with the question's own mark scheme

findings.claim: free will defined as 'The capacity to make choices independently of God's will'.
findings.truth: Loose wording. In Jewish teaching free will means a person's choices are not compelled by God, not that they fall outside God's will. The glossary entry in the same lesson states it correctly ('The capacity to make moral choices independently'), so the error is contained.
findings.evidence: internal inconsistency with the lesson glossary

findings.claim: Moses 'spoke with God "face to face, as a man speaks to his friend" (Exodus 33:11)'.
findings.truth: A modernised King James rendering ('as a man speaketh unto his friend'), not verbatim in any single standard translation. The substance and the reference are correct, so it is not worth an edit.
Both 1135 and 1138 are in wide circulation for Maimonides' birth year; 1138 is now the more common scholarly date. Neither is markable against a student.

findings.claim: Claims about examiner behaviour: 'exactly what the exam rewards' (L2 conclusion), 'the mark scheme rewards this contrast' (L2 exam tip), 'This is the texture the exam rewards' (L4 content).
findings.truth: The substance is supported: the spec requires common and divergent views within Judaism throughout, naming Orthodox, Reform and Liberal. Only the phrasing overclaims what a mark scheme says. No mark-affecting error, so no edit.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.6 preamble, 'Common and divergent views within Judaism ... should be included throughout'

findings.claim: All four lessons attach the instruction 'In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching' to the 6-mark Explain question, and all four exam tips tell students a source is compulsory there.
findings.truth: The spec fixes the marks (1, 1, 4, 6, 12) but never says which part carries the source instruction. If it in fact sits on a different part, all four lessons carry the same wrong instruction. Options: (a) leave it, since the source requirement has long sat on the longest AO1 part; (b) confirm against a current AQA specimen paper before the next flip and correct all four together. Recommend (a) plus a check by Tom - the risk is one shared instruction, not four separate errors.
findings.evidence: spec assessment sections, lines 264-271 and 1826-1836 (silent on the source instruction)
findings.ruling: Leave: matches the fleet convention / scenario stems read as valid.

findings.claim: Four practice questions use named-person scenario stems (Rachel in Leeds, Daniel in Manchester, Levi in north London, Miriam and her youth group).
findings.truth: This paper does not set scenario stems on the study-of-religions questions; the parts are direct ('Explain two ...'). The content of the questions is sound and the stems make good practice, but they teach a question shape the student will not meet. Options: (a) keep them as extra practice; (b) strip the scenario sentence from each of the four. Recommend (a) - the answers required are identical and rewriting four stems is not surgical.
findings.ruling: Leave: matches the fleet convention / scenario stems read as valid.

summary: One HIGH: lesson 3 teaches the Christian division of the Ten Commandments (four to God, six to people, with honouring parents among the duties to people) as the Jewish one, contradicting its own bein adam l'Makom / bein adam l'chavero section. Six MEDIUM fixes follow: four impossible 2-mark practice questions, a command-word mismatch on a 4-marker, an unsupported claim that tikkun olam appears in the Torah and the prophets, and one Talmud teaching cited two different ways inside a single lesson.
